clue.text: But those of a landowner do not ennoble him

definitions.text: But those of a landowner do not ennoble him

parts.words: But those of a landowner do not ennoble him
parts.note: plays on titled: a landowner holds papers with that word on them, yet holding them gives him no peerage

explanation.surface: A remark that owning land does not make a man a lord.
explanation.definitionFit: Documents proving ownership of property are deeds of title, which say nothing of rank.

clue.text: Drop in rent

explanation.surface: A drip in the rental price.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop of liquid shed from the eye, and a rip in cloth, share a spelling.

clue.text: But surely he doesn't throw away drink?

definitions.text: But surely he doesn't throw away drink?

parts.words: But surely he doesn't throw away drink?
parts.note: split as '...', throw away a vessel of drink, which is the last thing a heavy drinker would do

explanation.surface: Doubting that a certain man would ever waste his drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A drunkard, literally one who tosses back his pot of ale, would never waste it.

clue.text: Not necessarily a characteristic of the Oddfellows

definitions.text: Not necessarily a characteristic of the Oddfellows

parts.words: Not necessarily a characteristic of the Oddfellows
parts.note: the Oddfellows are a British friendly society, whose members need not really be odd or peculiar

explanation.surface: A remark that members of a friendly society are not necessarily strange.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oddfellows is a long-established British mutual aid society; despite the name, its members need not be strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddness or quirkiness of behaviour is the quality the society's name seems to promise.

clue.text: Old stagers in extortion?

parts.note: split as ..., former stage players, but those who demand money by force

explanation.surface: Retired performers turned to blackmail.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who demand payment by force are extortioners; split, the word suggests former performers.

clue.text: My dear! How fanciful!

indicators.note: an exclamation inviting us to ask how the words could be arranged, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at something whimsical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How' rearranges the letters of MY DEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lost in reverie is vague and given to imagination.

clue.text: America's responsibility?

parts.note: a duty that falls on the United States, so a burden in general

explanation.surface: A question about what the United States ought to take on.
explanation.definitionFit: A burden or duty resting on someone is that person's obligation, and here it rests on the US.

clue.text: What the novel of Victorian times has lost

definitions.text: What the novel of Victorian times has lost

parts.words: What the novel of Victorian times has lost
parts.note: novel seems to mean a book but means new; a fresh thing from the 1800s is no longer fresh

explanation.surface: A remark on how Victorian fiction has dated.
explanation.definitionFit: Freshness is what a once-novel thing loses as it ages.

clue.text: Lay emphasis on part played by siren

parts.note: a lay is a song or ballad
stress means emphasis

explanation.surface: A director stressing the role of the seductive singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' only links; the Sirens of legend lured sailors by singing, so a singer is the role they play.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sirens of Greek myth lured sailors with singing, so the part they played was that of a female singer.

clue.text: So it's a case, anyhow of people getting together

indicators.note: done anyhow means in no particular order, so the letters of the preceding words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A muddled remark that some matter is a case involving a gathering of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' rearranges the ten letters of SO IT'S A CASE; 'of' only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Partners or colleagues are people who have joined together in some enterprise.

clue.text: This song won't get an encore

definitions.text: This song won't get an encore

parts.words: This song won't get an encore
parts.note: a final performance is called by the name of a bird said to sing only once, as it dies

explanation.surface: A singer's number that the audience will not ask to hear again.
explanation.definitionFit: A last performance is a bird's song in the idiom, the legend being that the bird sings only when dying.

clue.text: A turning-point in urban development

parts.note: a turning-point here is literally a point where one turns, a junction in a built-up area

explanation.surface: A decisive moment for city planning.
explanation.definitionFit: Where two town roads meet is literally where one turns.

clue.text: Threads and yarns are

parts.note: fibres are twisted into thread, and stories are told at length, both described by the same past participle

explanation.surface: A plain statement about how textile threads are produced.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarn is twisted on a wheel and a tall tale is likewise drawn out, both by the verb's past participle.

clue.text: Impliedly the one woman Lord Darlington couldn't resist?

definitions.text: Impliedly the one woman Lord Darlington couldn't resist?

parts.words: Impliedly the one woman Lord Darlington couldn't resist?
parts.note: in Oscar Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan Lord Darlington says he can resist everything except temptation, so the woman would embody that

explanation.surface: A question about which lady could win over a character from a Wilde play.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Darlington, in Oscar Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan, famously says 'I can resist everything except temptation'; the female personification of that is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A seductive woman embodies temptation, the one thing Wilde's character admits he cannot resist.

clue.text: Brown study periods

parts.note: a brown study is a daydream, but this is Tom Brown, hero of a novel set at Rugby School

explanation.surface: Times of deep daydreaming.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'brown study' is a reverie, but Brown is Tom Brown of Thomas Hughes's novel of Rugby School life.
explanation.definitionFit: The years spent at school are when study happens, and Tom Brown's are the title of Hughes's novel.

clue.text: People tend to get fed up with their activities

definitions.text: People tend to get fed up with their activities

parts.words: People tend to get fed up with their activities
parts.note: fed up seems to mean bored, but read literally it means filled with food by those who supply meals

explanation.surface: A complaint that some people's doings make others weary.
explanation.definitionFit: Firms that supply food for functions leave their guests well fed.

clue.text: No rest when this muscle is twisted

indicators.note: something twisted is bent out of shape, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a pulled muscle gives no respite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is twisted' rearranges the six letters of NO REST.
explanation.definitionFit: A muscle that tightens or stretches a body part is named for the tension it produces.

clue.text: One allowed to have liquid assets

definitions.text: One allowed to have liquid assets

parts.words: One allowed to have liquid assets
parts.note: liquid assets seems financial, but means stock of drink that a publican is permitted to sell

explanation.surface: Someone permitted to keep cash readily available.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a pub landlord holds a licence to sell alcohol, so the 'liquid assets' are drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A publican holds official permission to sell alcohol, the drink being his stock.

clue.text: Where or how businessmen take their champagne?

definitions.text: Where or how businessmen take their champagne?

parts.words: Where or how businessmen take their champagne?
parts.note: the workplace of businessmen, and split as '...', the way chilled champagne is served

explanation.surface: A question about where executives drink their bubbly.
explanation.definitionFit: A businessman's workplace, which can also be split into two words describing chilled wine taken from its bucket.

clue.text: This smack doesn't hurt

parts.note: smack seems to be a blow but here means a taste, as in smacking of something

explanation.surface: A painless slap.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack can be a taste or savour, which causes no pain.

clue.text: Having no inclination to be languid

explanation.surface: Lacking the will to do anything and feeling sluggish.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads list as a lean or tilt, as of a ship, so 'having no list'.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally the word means without a tilt, as of a ship; in ordinary use it means lacking energy, limp and sluggish.

clue.text: Some footballers are always overweight

parts.note: ever means always
a ton is a huge weight, and someone said to weigh a ton is too heavy

explanation.surface: Players who are permanently carrying extra pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: EVERTON is a Liverpool football club.
explanation.definitionFit: A football club from Liverpool, so its players are some footballers.

clue.text: Boast about one encountered by a modern major-general

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for boasting goes round the letter for one

parts.note: to prate is to talk boastfully
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Bragging about a person met by a senior officer.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance, Major-General Stanley sings 'I am the very model of a modern Major-General' and meets the pirates.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Pirates of Penzance the Major-General faces a band of sea-robbers.

clue.text: Most stupid, at any rate

explanation.surface: Calling someone the dimmest, or at least so it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two it means having the smallest wisdom, that is dimmest; as one word it is an old adverb meaning at least.

clue.text: Frank suffering from exposure!

explanation.surface: Someone named Frank is in a bad way from the cold.
explanation.definitionFit: Candid speech is plain and unconcealed; something left uncovered is exposed to view or weather.

clue.text: Minus half of 20

indicators.note: half of a word means only one of its two halves is taken, here the back half

explanation.surface: Taking away half of twenty.
explanation.walkthrough: '20' refers to the answer of 20 across; the second half of its eight letters is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Minus means without or reduced by, as in 'ten minus two'.

clue.text: The small matter of a cat

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A minor issue concerning someone's pet.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiniest particle of an element is the smallest unit of matter.

clue.text: No estate, I'm switching to unpretentious dwelling

indicators.note: switching places means the letters of the preceding words change their positions

explanation.surface: Someone giving up a country estate to move into something humbler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switching' rearranges the ten letters of NO ESTATE I'M; 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A modest flat over two floors is a small home, the opposite of a grand estate.

clue.text: Kind that can be conned into marriage?

definitions.text: that can be conned into marriage?

explanation.surface: A type of person easily tricked into a wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is cryptic: put CON before this word and you get a spouse, so it is 'conned' into marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind is a type or variety; with con in front it becomes a word for a spouse.

clue.text: They're calculated to put people off

definitions.text: They're calculated to put people off

parts.words: They're calculated to put people off
parts.note: things deliberately designed to discourage attack or wrongdoing, such as weapons or penalties

explanation.surface: A remark about things meant to discourage people.
explanation.definitionFit: Weapons or punishments meant to discourage an enemy or offender are designed to dissuade.
